reference.source: Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder caused by an expanded CAG repeat in the ATN1 gene, making it a polyglutamine disease
It is comparatively common in Japanese populations and rarer elsewhere, so ethnic background and family history aid recognition
The phenotype depends strongly on age at onset: juvenile-onset disease resembles a progressive myoclonus epilepsy with seizures, myoclonus, and cognitive decline
Adult-onset disease is dominated by cerebellar ataxia, choreoathetosis, dementia, and psychiatric features
Marked anticipation occurs, with larger repeat expansions transmitted particularly through the paternal line producing earlier and more severe disease in offspring
The clinical overlap with other ataxias and with Huntington disease means genetic testing is important for accurate diagnosis
MRI typically shows atrophy of the cerebellum and brainstem, and white matter changes may be present, especially in older patients
Diagnosis is confirmed by detecting the pathological CAG repeat expansion in ATN1, and management is supportive including seizure control
reference.pathophysiology: Dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy is a polyglutamine disorder caused by an expanded CAG repeat in ATN1, which encodes atrophin-1. The elongated polyglutamine tract leads to protein misfolding and nuclear accumulation that is toxic to neurons, with degeneration concentrated in the dentatorubral and pallidoluysian systems as the name indicates. Longer repeat expansions produce earlier onset and more severe disease, and paternal transmission tends to increase repeat size, explaining the pronounced anticipation and the shift toward the juvenile epileptic phenotype in successive generations.
additionalDifferentials: Other inherited and acquired cerebellar ataxias
additionalInvestigations: ATN1 CAG repeat analysis as the confirmatory test
Brain MRI to assess cerebellar, brainstem, and white matter changes
EEG in patients with seizures and myoclonus
Detailed pedigree analysis to identify anticipation and inheritance pattern
redFlags: Refractory seizures or status in juvenile-onset disease
Severe ataxia with falls and injury
Prominent psychiatric disturbance requiring urgent management
reference.prognosis: The disorder is progressive with no curative therapy; juvenile-onset disease tends to progress more rapidly and severely, whereas adult-onset disease advances more slowly, and overall survival is shortened with care remaining supportive.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as Huntington disease or another spinocerebellar ataxia without genetic confirmation
Overlooking DRPLA in the differential of progressive myoclonus epilepsy in children
Failing to counsel families about anticipation and paternal transmission risk
Attributing white matter changes to an unrelated process
management: No disease-modifying therapy exists; care is supportive and directed at the individual symptom pattern
Control seizures and myoclonus with anticonvulsants such as valproate, levetiracetam and clonazepam, avoiding agents that aggravate myoclonus
Manage chorea and other movement disorder with dopamine-depleting agents such as tetrabenazine or antidopaminergic drugs
Treat associated psychiatric features including depression and psychosis and provide cognitive support
Provide physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech and language therapy for ataxia, mobility and swallowing, with nutritional support
Coordinate neurology, rehabilitation and palliative care within a multidisciplinary team as the disease advances
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance and anticipation, including predictive testing for at-risk relatives
